title: Profit From Every Upswing
statement:
prices[i] is the price of one share on day i. You may trade as often as you like, but you can hold at most one share at a time: you must sell before you buy again. Selling and then buying on the same day is allowed.

Return the largest total profit you can make. If no trade makes money, return 0.

examples.why: Buy at 3, sell at 8 (+5), buy at 2, sell at 9 (+7). The best single trade, 2 → 9, only makes 7.
The price only falls, so the best plan is to never buy.
One trade from 2 to 8 earns the same as three one-day trades of +2 each.

hints: Since trades are unlimited, think about what a long trade from day a to day b is made of.
A trade from a to b earns exactly the sum of the day-to-day changes between them. Which of those changes do you want?
Add up every positive difference prices[i] − prices[i − 1]. Each one is a one-day trade worth taking.

explain.intuition:
Any trade from day a to day b earns prices[b] − prices[a], which is the sum of the daily changes in between. If some of those daily changes are negative, you would do better by stepping out on the down days. With unlimited trades you can always do that.

So the best plan collects every rising day and skips every falling one. The answer is the sum of all positive differences between neighbouring days. Selling and rebuying on the same day is free, which is why gluing one-day trades together equals one long trade.
steps: For every day i from 1 on, compute prices[i] − prices[i − 1].
If it is positive, add it to profit.
pitfalls: Solving the single-trade version (max price minus earlier min). In [3, 8, 2, 6, 9] that gives 7, not 12.
Trying to find exact valleys and peaks with fiddly index logic. The sum of positive differences gives the same total with no edge cases.
Adding negative differences too, which just gives last price minus first price.

solutions.title: Two states per day
solutions.idea: Track the best money you can have at the end of each day while holding a share and while holding none. Each day either keeps its state or trades into the other.

solutions.title: Sum of rising days
solutions.idea: Every long profitable trade splits into one-day rises. Take every positive day-to-day difference.

followups: Each sale now costs a fixed fee. Why does the sum-of-rises trick break, and how does the two-state version handle it?
You may make at most two trades. What states do you need then?
